stories.title: What’s Driving CMBS Distress in the Top U.S. Metro Areas
stories.excerpt: Across the 50 largest commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) markets, $45.8 billion of $393.5 billion in outstanding balance is currently distressed, a balance-weighted rate of 11.6 percent, according to CRED iQ data. Minneapolis, Denver and Oklahoma City lead the distress rankings at 55.1 percent, 35.9 percent and 34.1 percent, respectively, each shaped by a handful of very large loans rather than broader weakness, while Salt Lake City sits at zero, and is therefore the cleanest metro in the top 50. Underneath it all, the property type driving distress has shifted. Multifamily distress has more than doubled since February, from 6 percent to 13 percent, while office distress has eased off from 21.2 percent to 16.7 percent. Minneapolis, Denver and Oklahoma City top the list of most distressed metropolitan areas, followed by Portland, Ore. (30.6 percent), Austin (28.7 percent), and a cluster of Midwest metros, specifically Chicago (26.4 percent), Cleveland (23.6 percent) and Milwaukee (23.1 percent), plus San Francisco (21.5 percent). At the other end of the spectrum, Phoenix, Boston, Las Vegas and Orlando, Fla., all sit around 3 percent, with San Diego and Salt Lake City as the most stable large markets at 0.4 percent and zero percent, respectively. Office remains the largest source of cumulative distress at 16.7 percent ($22.5 billion, roughly half of all distressed balance nationally), followed by mixed-use (14.4 percent), multifamily (13 percent), lodging (10.6 percent) and retail (8.8 percent). Industrial is the clear outperformer at just 1 percent. Regionally, the Midwest’s 10 metros average 22.7 percent distress, driven by concentrated issues in Minneapolis, Chicago, St. Louis, Cleveland, Milwaukee and Cincinnati, while the Northeast, West and South all cluster near 10 percent. bullets: Multifamily distress doubled Feb–now: 6% to 13% of CMBS portfolio balance
Minneapolis 55.1%, Denver 35.9%, Oklahoma City 34.1% distressed; Salt Lake City 0%
Office distress eased 21.2% to 16.7%; property-type shift signals refinance cliff risk
stories.summary: Across 50 largest U.S. CMBS markets, $45.8B of $393.5B outstanding (11.6%) is distressed. Multifamily distress has accelerated sharply—doubling since February—while office distress has moderated. Minneapolis, Denver, and Oklahoma City lead national distress rankings, driven by oversized legacy loans rather than broad market weakness. The shift in distressed property type from office to multifamily marks a critical turning point in the commercial real estate cycle.
stories.impact: This acceleration in multifamily CMBS distress signals refinance maturity risk and asset-sale pressure across major metros, particularly Minneapolis, Denver, Oklahoma City, Austin, and Chicago. Developers should anticipate 12–18 month window of forced-sale inventory and depressed cap rates in these markets as lenders work through problem loans, creating acquisition opportunities but also competitive pricing pressure on development land. Conversely, low-distress metros (Phoenix, Boston, Las Vegas, Orlando at ~3%) remain tight for land and underwriting spreads.

stories.title: Barings Provides $86M Acquisition Debt for Charleston Industrial Portfolio
stories.excerpt: Obelisk Real Estate Partners has secured $86.2 million to finance the acquisition of a three-building industrial portfolio in Charleston, South Carolina, Commercial Observer can first report. Barings provided the debt, while JLL’s Peter Rotchford, Christopher Peck, and Nicholas Thorton arranged the transaction. The seller was CenterPoint Properties. Ryan Naumes, managing director with Barings, noted in a statement that his firm has a previous relationship with Obelisk and that the portfolio is located in “one of the Southeast’s most compelling industrial markets.” “With a logistics and port-oriented location, the portfolio aligns well with our focus on high-quality industrial real estate in markets with durable demand drivers,” said Naumes. Spanning roughly 817,000 square feet across three assets, the portfolio is presently 62 percent leased, with Obelisk Real Estate Partners set to initiate a value-add investment plan through new capital improvements. Both Obelisk and Barings cited its advantageous location. Through Interstate-26 and Interstate-526, the portfolio is connected to the demand drivers like the Port of Charleston, North Charleston Terminal, and a Boeing production facility. “Charleston’s industrial sector continues to show strong momentum, making it a focus market for Obelisk,” said Jake Meskin, acquisitions associate with Obelisk Real Estate Partners. Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Barings finances $86.2M acquisition debt for Obelisk's 817K-SF Charleston industrial portfolio
Three-building portfolio 62% leased; CenterPoint seller; value-add repositioning planned
Charleston logistics/port orientation cited as high-conviction buy thesis
stories.summary: Obelisk Real Estate Partners acquired a three-building, 817,000-square-foot industrial portfolio in Charleston, South Carolina, financed by Barings with $86.2M in debt. The portfolio, previously owned by CenterPoint Properties, is currently 62% leased and targeted for value-add repositioning through capital improvements. Barings highlighted Charleston's logistics and port-oriented location as a durable demand driver justifying the acquisition.
stories.impact: Charleston industrial market continues to attract institutional debt and equity capital, reinforcing its position as a supply-constrained port-logistics hub with secular tailwinds from e-commerce and manufacturing reshoring. Multifamily developers in Charleston should expect sustained demand from in-migrating logistics and distribution workforce; industrial absorption will tighten land availability and raise acquisition costs in submarkets near port/rail corridors.

stories.title: Equity Residential and AvalonBay: Inside the $71B Mega Multifamily Merger
stories.excerpt: On May 21, shortly before Memorial Day weekend, participants in public real estate markets awoke to a truly remarkable headline. AvalonBay Communities, the owner of 98,000 apartments and with a market capitalization of $25 billion, would be merging with Equity Residential, one of the oldest real estate investment trusts (REITs) in America, holding 85,000 apartments and $20.5 billion assets under management. “The initial reaction was, ‘Holy cow, two of the largest, most storied apartment REIT companies nationally are choosing to merge,’” said Allan Swaringen, president and CEO of JLL Income Property Trust, a REIT. “These are the two biggest gorillas in the multifamily marketplace who decided to come together. It’s a true merger of equals.” With a total enterprise value of roughly $71 billion, the deal marks the single largest public REIT merger ever, dwarfing the 2022 deal between Prologis and Duke Realty valued at $26 billion. The two apartment firms announced in late July their new company will be called Vivmark Residential. Once the all-stock merger is complete later this year, this new multifamily behemoth will own more than 180,000 rental apartments across more than 600 communities in the U.S. — mainly in the largest coastal cities — plus another 10,800 apartments and $4.4 billion under construction across 32 communities, of which 50 percent will hold an affordable or mixed-income component, the firms noted in a shared release. “My first reaction is they should’ve done it a few years ago. It’s a very natural merger,” said Matt Frankel, a stock market analyst at the Motley Fool, who noted that roughly 95 percent of Equity Residential and AvalonBay’s businesses operate out of the same markets, mainly New York, San Francisco, Boston and Washington, D.C. Equity is headquartered out of Chicago, while AvalonBay calls Arlington, Va., home. “This would be like if Visa or Mastercard were allowed to merge. bullets: Equity Residential + AvalonBay merge: $71B enterprise value; 183K apartments combined
Largest public REIT merger ever; creates dominant portfolio with operational scale
Market consolidation signals confidence in multifamily fundamentals despite rate/cap-rate headwinds
stories.summary: Equity Residential (85K apartments, $20.5B AUM) and AvalonBay Communities (98K apartments, $25B market cap) announced a merger of equals valued at $71 billion enterprise value—the largest public REIT merger on record. The combined entity will own and operate 183,000 apartments across major U.S. markets. Industry observers characterized the deal as a merger of the two largest multifamily operators in America, signaling confidence in long-term rental fundamentals despite near-term cap-rate pressures.
stories.impact: Mega-REIT consolidation removes two independent competitors from the acquisition market and creates a behemoth with pricing power, operational scale, and balance-sheet capacity for land banking and forward development in prime markets. For smaller and mid-cap developers, this signals: (1) public-market confidence in multifamily despite rate uncertainty; (2) likely intensified acquisition competition from combined EQR/AVB in core markets (CA, TX, NY, FL, Southeast); and (3) potential opportunity for developers to sell stabilized assets to the enlarged REIT or to fill niche supply gaps that the mega-REIT underserves (secondary markets, workforce, active-adult).

stories.title: Sunday Summary: Seven. Hundred. Fifty. Billion.
stories.excerpt: Three-quarters of a trillion dollars can buy you pretty much anything you want. If you took the gross national product of Chile, and added the GNP of Colombia, you’d still have more than $100 billion left — and that can also get you pretty much anything in the known world. Well, J.P. Morgan Chase has decided to use that ungodly amount of lucre to invest it in a roof over one’s head. On Monday, the bank announced an unprecedented push to build $750 billion worth of housing over the next nine years with the goal of increasing both supply and homeownership nationwide. (Oh, yeah — Commercial Observer broke the story.) “We’re focused on helping more people access quality housing they can afford,” said Michelle Herrick, the bank’s head of commercial real estate. “And we’re working across the real estate community, local governments and nonprofits to scale housing solutions throughout the U.S.” J.P. Morgan’s approach will be to focus on expanding financing through debt, equity and grants, with a target of creating 1 million units of affordable housing. They’re hoping to aid 500,000 customers, of which they’re anticipating 200,000 will be first-time buyers. Of course, the timing of this is opportune. Back in May, CO reported that construction starts on multifamily projects throughout the U.S. for the first quarter of this year hadn’t been this low since 2011. But a few companies have been trying to meet the demand — at least in certain regions. In New York, for example, LMXD and Bedrock Real Estate Partners are building a 560-unit mixed-income development in Astoria. In Florida, Ultimate Equity just shelled out $32 million for a 69-unit townhome community in Hollywood. Krea USA is mid-construction on a 385-unit development called Le Parc at Lauderhill in Lauderhill, Fla. And Harbor Group International bought a zoo — actually, make that HGI bought a garden-style apartment complex near Zoo Miami. bullets: JPMorgan Chase commits $750B housing investment over 9 years; 1M affordable units target
Debt, equity, grant capital; 500K customer assistance goal; unprecedented scale commitment
Addresses systemic supply shortage and affordability crisis through major lender capital mobilization
stories.summary: J.P. Morgan Chase announced a $750 billion housing investment initiative over nine years targeting 1 million units of affordable housing creation and assistance to 500,000 customers. The bank will deploy capital across debt, equity, and grant vehicles in partnership with local governments and nonprofits. This represents an unprecedented commitment by a single institution to address national housing supply and affordability shortfalls.
stories.impact: JPMorgan's $750B commitment signals institutional recognition that housing supply crisis demands non-traditional (equity/grant) capital alongside traditional debt, and will reshape development financing landscape. Developers should expect: (1) new debt and equity capital sources earmarked for workforce/affordable multifamily in secondary and tertiary markets; (2) lower required equity returns on affordable/mixed-income deals; (3) potential grant funding for predevelopment/infrastructure in affordable-friendly submarkets; (4) increased regulatory/political pressure on all lenders to follow JPMorgan's lead, improving term availability for mission-driven projects in tight markets like CA, NY, CO, NC.

stories.title: Selldorf Architects Signs Long-Term Renewal at 860 Broadway
stories.excerpt: Colliers SVP Seth Hecht has secured a 10-year, 13,815-square-foot lease renewal for architecture firm Selldorf Architects at 860 Broadway. Hecht represented Gordon Property Group in completing the long-term renewal transaction. Selldorf Architects was represented by Erik Schmall and Scott Weiss of Savills. Led by internationally acclaimed architect Annabelle Selldorf, the firm has called 860 Broadway home for the past two decades. “860 Broadway is one of Manhattan’s iconic office buildings, and its location continues to make it a highly desirable destination for creative and innovative companies,” said Hecht. “When a firm as globally respected as Selldorf Architects commits to another decade in the building, it speaks to both the property’s enduring appeal and the long-term strength of this market.” In addition to Selldorf Architects, current 860 Broadway tenants include Industrious, Valon and retail tenant Uniqlo. Hecht is also representing Gordon Property Group in leasing three additional Manhattan office properties. The post Selldorf Architects Signs Long-Term Renewal at 860 Broadway appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Selldorf Architects renews 13,815 SF for 10 years at 860 Broadway Manhattan
Global architecture firm commits to two-decade-long occupancy; iconic trophy office location
Tenant renewal signals strength in creative/design office market despite broader sector headwinds
stories.summary: Architecture firm Selldorf Architects renewed a 10-year lease for 13,815 square feet at 860 Broadway in Manhattan, representing a long-term commitment by the internationally acclaimed practice. The firm has occupied the space for two decades. Current tenants at the iconic building include Industrious, Valon, and retail tenant Uniqlo.
stories.impact: Minimal direct relevance to multifamily development. The renewal signals resilience in trophy-office submarkets (Flatiron/Union Square) for firms with strong brand equity and creative tenants, but does not affect apartment demand, supply, capital, or construction costs. For context: 860 Broadway occupancy remains selective and skews toward high-income creative/professional users; this renewal reflects captive brand loyalty rather than broad-market office recovery.

stories.title: Innocean USA Signs 100K-SF lease with Hackman Capital in Headquarters Relocation
stories.excerpt: Advertising agency Innocean USA has signed a new 101,000-square-foot office lease at Hackman Capital Partners’ 888 N. Douglas property in El Segundo. The space will serve as the company’s U.S. headquarters and represents a relocation from 50,000 square feet of space in Huntington Beach. The tenant will move into its new space after construction concludes in 2027. JLL’s Jason Fine, Jeff Ingham, and Mitch Lundquist represented Innocean USA in the new lease. Hackman Capital represented itself. “This is a transformative change for Innocean USA, and we spent years advising the leadership team to help find a ‘one of one’ facility that would bring their company vision of the future to reality,” said Fine. “This is going to be a special place where their employees and creativity will absolutely thrive.”  Across from the Lakers’ practice facility and the L.A. Times headquarters, 888 Douglas is a 30-acre campus with four buildings totaling approximately 550,000 square feet. Hackman Capital purchased the 1930s-era aerospace manufacturing site in 2016 and invested $100 million to transform it into a creative office campus. Image courtesy of Gensler. The post Innocean USA Signs 100K-SF lease with Hackman Capital in Headquarters Relocation appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Innocean USA signs 101K-SF HQ lease at Hackman Capital's 888 N. Douglas, El Segundo
Relocation from 50K SF Huntington Beach; move-in 2027 post-construction; doubling footprint
Employer expansion in LA aerospace/creative campus indicates regional talent/HQ consolidation trend
stories.summary: Advertising agency Innocean USA leased 101,000 square feet at Hackman Capital Partners' 888 N. Douglas campus in El Segundo, California, more than doubling its prior 50,000-square-foot footprint in Huntington Beach. The tenant will occupy the space following construction completion in 2027. The 30-acre campus, a converted 1930s aerospace manufacturing site, includes four buildings totaling ~550,000 square feet.
stories.impact: Innocean's HQ expansion and consolidation to El Segundo signals continued inward migration of advertising/creative services to Los Angeles metro and suggests sustained corporate tenant appetite for specialized creative campuses in Southland. Multifamily developers in LA Harbor Area/El Segundo/Manhattan Beach submarkets should anticipate upstream demand from agency employee in-migration and talent recruitment; target workforce housing (100K–$150K income, families with children, proximity to creative jobs) in beach communities and near LAX corridor over next 24–36 months.

stories.title: MADDD Equities Scoops Up Vacant West Farms Industrial
stories.excerpt: Ariel Property Advisors closed the sale of 425 Devoe Ave., a vacant multi-story industrial property in the West Farms neighborhood of The Bronx, for $10,750,000. The property spans 60,000 square feet above grade, which translates to $180 per square foot, with an additional 30,000 square feet below grade. An Ariel investment sales team led by senior director Jason M. Gold, along with partner Sean R. Kelly, Esq. and director Daniel Mahfa represented the seller, Abingdon Square Partners. The buyer was MADDD Equities, LLC. “The sale of 425 Devoe Ave. demonstrates the strong demand for large, commercial sites offering convenient regional access,” said Gold. Situated on a 40,097-square-foot lot, the property features four levels of usable industrial and warehouse space. It is located near the 2 and 5 subway lines and offers convenient access to the Cross Bronx Expressway, Sheridan Boulevard and the broader New York region. The post MADDD Equities Scoops Up Vacant West Farms Industrial appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: MADDD Equities acquires vacant West Farms industrial, Bronx, for $10.75M ($180/SF)
60K SF above grade + 30K SF below; 40K-SF lot; near subway + Cross Bronx Expressway
Large commercial site repositioning signals Bronx industrial market recovery and adaptive-use potential
stories.summary: MADDD Equities purchased 425 Devoe Ave., a vacant four-story industrial property in the Bronx's West Farms neighborhood, for $10.75 million ($180 per square foot above grade). The 60,000-square-foot above-grade structure (with an additional 30,000 square feet below grade) sits on a 40,097-square-foot lot with proximity to the 2 and 5 subway lines and the Cross Bronx Expressway. The property was sold by Abingdon Square Partners.
stories.impact: Bronx industrial repositioning and vacant-building acquisition at $180/SF signals emerging investor confidence in Outer-Borough logistics/manufacturing conversion and light-industrial redevelopment. Multifamily developers should note: (1) large industrial sites in accessible Bronx submarkets (West Farms, South Bronx) with transit/highway access are entering redevelopment pipeline; (2) potential for adaptive-use mixed-income/affordable multifamily conversions on industrial sites as Bronx gentrification pressures increase; (3) workforce housing demand from industrial/logistics job retention and new creative/tech tenants will drive rental demand in adjacent residential submarkets; (4) zoning/entitlement risk remains high, but approval speed improving—opportunity to acquire repositionable industrial sites before land values fully adjust.

stories.title: Shopoff Secures Approval for Buena Park Residential Development
stories.excerpt: Shopoff Realty Investments has secured unanimous approval from the Buena Park City Council for 5600 Beach Blvd, a 13.76-acre residential development in Buena Park. The property is currently occupied by the Amway Corporation with a corporate sale-leaseback in place until the end of 2026 and consists of two industrial buildings totaling approximately 370,031 square feet. “5600 Beach Blvd represents an important step forward for Orange County and is intended to help address the need for attainable and diverse housing options for first-time homebuyers and for Buena Park’s growing senior population,” said Shopoff Realty Investments’ president and CEO, Bill Shopoff. “Transforming an industrial site into a vibrant residential community aligns with the city and county’s evolving needs, providing homes for people at every stage of life.” The development aims to deliver 231 three-story townhomes and duplex units, offered with four different floor plans, along with 50 for-rent senior affordable housing units. Homes are expected to be delivered in 2029-2030. Where the apartment industry connects. Meet the owners, investors, developers, lenders, brokers, and service providers driving today’s multifamily market at Connect Apartments. Build relationships, uncover opportunities, and stay ahead of what’s next. The post Shopoff Secures Approval for Buena Park Residential Development appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Shopoff Realty secures unanimous Buena Park council approval for 5600 Beach Blvd; 13.76 acres
231 townhomes/duplexes + 50 senior affordable units; delivery 2029–2030; Amway sale-leaseback to 2026
Industrial-to-residential conversion addresses Orange County affordability/senior-housing gap
stories.summary: Shopoff Realty Investments won unanimous approval from Buena Park City Council for a 13.76-acre residential development at 5600 Beach Blvd. The project transforms two industrial buildings (370,031 SF, currently leased to Amway through 2026) into 231 three-story townhomes and duplexes plus 50 for-rent senior affordable units across four floor plans. Deliveries are projected for 2029–2030.
stories.impact: Buena Park industrial-to-residential conversion and city-approved entitlement pipeline signal Orange County market willingness to rezone industrial land for housing and seniors, reducing nimbyism barriers in historically industrial-zoned OC submarkets. Multifamily developers in Orange County should: (1) prioritize acquisition of industrial/vacant parcels in Buena Park, Anaheim, Santa Ana with near-term leaseback exits; (2) expect 18–24 month approval timelines for similar TOD/affordable mixed-income projects given city/county political alignment on housing supply; (3) compete on senior-affordable units as county demographic shift (aging in place) and state policies (state senior housing credits) drive subsidy availability and cap-rate compression for workforce/senior products.

stories.title: Matawan Retail Trades to Private Investor for $15M
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap completed the sale of Park Plaza, a retail center in Matawan, NJ. The asset sold for $14.67 million. “Park Plaza attracted significant investor interest due to its diverse tenant mix, strong visibility and strategic location within one of Monmouth County’s most established retail corridors,” said Seth Goldberg, associate director investments in Marcus & Millichap’s New Jersey office. “Well-positioned neighborhood shopping centers with durable cash flow continue to be highly sought after, and this transaction reflects the sustained demand for quality retail assets in New Jersey.” Goldberg, Brent Hyldahl and Alan Cafiero of Marcus & Millichap marketed the property for the seller and procured the buyer, both private investors from New Jersey. Located at 343-351 State Rte. 34, the retail center sits on a 5.86-acre lot totaling 61,750 square feet. It was built in 1986 and contains 20 suites. The rent roll features a diverse mix of dining, lifestyle, retail and service-oriented tenants, including a Dunkin’ with a drive-thru. The post Matawan Retail Trades to Private Investor for $15M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Marcus & Millichap closed $14.67M sale of Park Plaza retail center, Matawan, NJ (61.75K SF)
20-suite neighborhood shopping center; 1986 vintage; diverse tenants including Dunkin' drive-thru
Retail-center investor appetite remains resilient for durable-cash-flow neighborhood assets
stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap brokered the $14.67 million sale of Park Plaza, a 61,750-square-foot retail center in Matawan, New Jersey, to a private investor. Built in 1986 on 5.86 acres, the 20-suite property features a diverse tenant mix including dining, lifestyle, retail, and service tenants (including a Dunkin' with drive-thru). Both buyer and seller were New Jersey-based private investors.
stories.impact: Minimal direct relevance to multifamily development. Retail sales data shows selective investor demand persists for neighborhood centers with diversified cash-flow tenants and drive-thru/durables exposure, but does not affect multifamily supply, demand, or capital availability. Asset class remains secondary to institutional multifamily and industrial capital flows.

stories.title: Longfellow Sells Hatch Life Sciences Building in LIC for $87M
stories.excerpt: Life sciences developer Longfellow Real Estate Partners has parted with its first-ever New York City project at a discount. Longfellow’s Hatch Life Sciences Building, located at 43-10 23 Street in Long Island City, Queens, has sold for $86.9 million, according to city records filed Friday. Pearl Realty Management’s Jack Guttman signed for the buyer, under the entity 4310 23 St. A representative of Pearl Realty Management did not respond to requests for comment. Longfellow purchased the existing building at 43-10 23 Street in 2021 alongside its partner, Steven Orbuch’s Sculptor Real Estate, for $92.5 million. Longfellow, led by CEO and co-founder Adam Sichol, planned to invest another $120 million into turning the former parachute manufacturing plant into a mix of life sciences labs and offices. Construction had all but wrapped up when Commercial Observer visited in 2024. The final product spanned over 208,000 square feet across seven floors, including prebuilt lab suites, modular research space and flexible office areas. Longfellow and Sculptor did not respond immediately to requests for comment on the sale. While Guttman’s plans for the purchase remain unclear, the landlord appears to be active in the Long Island City market. Recent purchases include the Standard Motors Product Building at 37-18 Northern Boulevard for $42 million and BrightSpire Capital‘s office building at 21-02 49th Avenue for $28 million. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Longfellow Real Estate sells Hatch Life Sciences Building, LIC Queens, for $86.9M (loss)
Purchased 2021 for $92.5M + $120M capex; 208K-SF mixed lab/office; buyer Pearl Realty Management
Life-sciences market cooling; speculative repositioning underperforms; exit signals investor thesis retreat
stories.summary: Longfellow Real Estate Partners sold its Hatch Life Sciences Building at 43-10 23 Street in Long Island City, Queens, for $86.9 million—a loss from its $92.5 million acquisition price in 2021 alongside partner Steven Orbuch's Sculptor Real Estate. The developer had planned $120 million in capital to convert the former parachute manufacturing facility into 208,000 square feet of prebuilt lab suites, modular research space, and flexible office. Pearl Realty Management acquired the stabilized asset.
stories.impact: Longfellow's below-cost exit from NYC life-sciences signals cooling demand/cap-rate expansion in speculative lab-office conversions; perceived structural supply excess or tenant-credit weakness in LIC life-sciences market. For multifamily developers: (1) life-sciences anchor strategies in mixed-use development face headwind; (2) LIC office/lab oversupply likely to suppress nearby multifamily rents and impede co-tenancy support for larger residential projects; (3) repurposing of life-sciences-targeted real estate (conversion back to generic office/flex or to residential) may accelerate, opening adaptive-use multifamily opportunities on Queens waterfront but with extended leasing timelines and higher concession risk.
